title: Driver Out of Memory: java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
summary: The Spark driver JVM exhausts its heap, usually after collecting a large result set to the driver or broadcasting an oversized table. The notebook detaches and the cluster reports the driver as unresponsive.
issue:
A job or notebook fails with java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space raised on the driver.

Typical log evidence:
ERROR Executor: Exception in task ... java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
ERROR SparkContext: Error initializing SparkContext
The spark driver has stopped unexpectedly and is restarting. Your notebook will be automatically reattached.

The driver log often shows a long run of full GC pauses immediately before the failure.
cause:
The driver JVM heap is exhausted. The three dominant causes, in order of frequency:

1. Collecting too much data to the driver. Calls to collect(), toPandas(), take(n) with a large n, or displaying a very wide result pull all partitions into driver memory.
2. Broadcast join of an oversized table. The optimizer chose a broadcast because statistics were stale; the broadcast table is materialized in full on the driver before distribution.
3. Too many partitions or tasks. The driver holds task metadata for every task; jobs with hundreds of thousands of partitions can exhaust heap on bookkeeping alone.
environment: All Lakehouse Runtime versions. All cloud providers. Applies to both all-purpose and job clusters.
resolution:
1. Identify what is being pulled to the driver
Search the notebook or job source for collect(), toPandas(), and display() on unaggregated DataFrames. Replace collect() with write to a Delta table, or with limit(n).collect() where n is bounded.

2. Check for an unintended broadcast join
Run EXPLAIN FORMATTED on the failing query and look for BroadcastHashJoin against a table you expect to be large. If present, either refresh statistics with ANALYZE TABLE <table> COMPUTE STATISTICS or disable auto-broadcast for the job:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", -1)

3. Increase driver memory
Move the cluster to a node type with more driver memory. Prefer a memory-optimized driver over simply enlarging the whole cluster; workers are rarely the constraint in this failure mode.

4. Reduce partition count
If the job has an unusually high task count, set spark.sql.shuffle.partitions to a value near 2-3x the total core count rather than leaving it at a large manual override.

5. Confirm the fix
Re-run the job and check the driver log for full GC entries. A healthy run shows no repeated Full GC (Allocation Failure) lines in the final minutes.

title: ExecutorLostFailure: Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits
summary: Executors are terminated by the resource manager for exceeding their memory allocation. The stage retries and eventually the job aborts after four attempts.
issue:
A stage fails repeatedly and the job aborts with:

ERROR TaskSetManager: Task 47 in stage 12.0 failed 4 times; aborting job
ExecutorLostFailure (executor 7 exited caused by one of the running tasks) Reason: Container killed by YARN for exceeding memory limits. 28.4 GB of 28 GB physical memory used.

The Spark UI shows a small number of tasks with very large shuffle read sizes relative to the median.
cause: An individual executor exceeded its container memory limit. This is almost always a symptom of skew rather than an under-provisioned cluster: a few partitions hold far more data than the rest, so a handful of tasks demand disproportionate memory. Secondary causes include large Python UDF memory overhead not accounted for in the JVM allocation, and caching a DataFrame that does not fit in the configured storage fraction.
environment: Lakehouse Runtime 10.4 LTS and above. Most commonly seen on jobs performing wide joins or aggregations on keys with a heavy hitter value such as a null placeholder or a default tenant ID.
resolution:
1. Confirm skew before resizing anything
In the Spark UI, open the failing stage and compare the max task shuffle read against the 75th percentile. A ratio above roughly 10x confirms skew.

2. Enable adaptive query execution skew handling
On DBR 10.4+ this is on by default, but verify it was not disabled:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", true)
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", true)

3. Isolate the heavy key
Run a count grouped by the join key and inspect the top values. Null and sentinel values are the usual culprits. Filter them out and handle them separately, or salt the key by appending a bounded random suffix on both sides of the join.

4. Increase memory overhead for Python workloads
If the job uses Python UDFs or pandas UDFs, raise the off-heap allowance:
spark.executor.memoryOverhead 4g

5. Only then resize
If skew is genuinely absent and every task is large, move to a memory-optimized worker type. Adding more workers of the same size will not help, because the constraint is per-container.

title: Cluster launch failure: INSTANCE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED or CLOUD_PROVIDER_LAUNCH_FAILURE
summary: A cluster fails to start because the cloud account has hit an instance, vCPU, or IP address quota. The platform event log records the provider error verbatim.
issue:
A cluster never reaches RUNNING and terminates with one of:

TERMINATED: INSTANCE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED
CLOUD_PROVIDER_LAUNCH_FAILURE: The cloud provider launch failed. Error code: InstanceLimitExceeded
Error: VcpuLimitExceeded - You have requested more vCPU capacity than your current vCPU limit

The cluster event log shows the request being retried and then abandoned. Jobs scheduled against the cluster fail with a cluster-unavailable message rather than an application error.
cause:
The underlying cloud account cannot satisfy the instance request. Distinct sub-causes:

1. Service quota reached for the instance family in that region (AWS vCPU limits are per instance family, not per account).
2. Subnet IP exhaustion in the workspace VPC or VNet. Each node consumes at least one private IP; autoscaling clusters can drain a small subnet quickly.
3. Capacity unavailable in the availability zone, which is transient and distinct from a quota problem.
4. Spot capacity unavailable when the cluster is configured for spot with no on-demand fallback.
environment: All workspaces. Most common on AWS with default per-family vCPU limits, and on Azure where regional vCPU quotas are set per subscription and per VM series.
resolution:
1. Read the exact provider error code
Open the cluster, go to the Event Log tab, and expand the termination event. Distinguish a quota error (InstanceLimitExceeded, VcpuLimitExceeded, QuotaExceeded) from a capacity error (InsufficientInstanceCapacity). They have different fixes.

2. For a quota error, request an increase
Raise the service quota for the specific instance family and region in the cloud console. Note the request applies to the family, so switching from an r5 to an i3 node type may work immediately as a stopgap.

3. For a capacity error, change zone or node type
Set the cluster availability zone to auto so the platform can place the request where capacity exists, or select a different node type in the same class.

4. For subnet IP exhaustion
Check available IPs in the workspace subnets. A cluster needs at least (workers + 1) addresses. Either expand the subnet CIDR or lower the cluster max workers.

5. For spot failures
Enable on-demand fallback on the cluster, or reduce the spot ratio so the driver and a baseline of workers are on-demand.

6. Prevent recurrence
Set a max workers value on autoscaling clusters that fits within the quota, and use cluster policies to cap instance counts across the workspace.

title: Unity Catalog PERMISSION_DENIED when querying a table or schema
summary: A query fails with PERMISSION_DENIED even though the user appears to have access. The cause is nearly always a missing USE CATALOG or USE SCHEMA grant along the object path, or a cluster in a non-UC access mode.
issue:
A query against a Unity Catalog table fails with:

org.apache.spark.sql.AnalysisException: [INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS] Insufficient privileges: User does not have permission SELECT on table 'main.sales.transactions'

or

PERMISSION_DENIED: User does not have USE SCHEMA on Schema 'main.sales'

The user reports that they were granted SELECT on the table and cannot understand why access still fails.
cause:
Unity Catalog privileges are hierarchical and non-inheriting upward. Holding SELECT on a table is not sufficient; the principal must also hold USE CATALOG on the parent catalog and USE SCHEMA on the parent schema. Granting only the leaf privilege is the single most common misconfiguration.

Two other causes produce the same error text:

1. The cluster is in No Isolation Shared or a legacy access mode that cannot pass user identity to Unity Catalog. Only Shared and Single User access modes are UC-enabled.
2. The external location or storage credential backing the table does not grant the principal READ FILES, which surfaces as a permission error at query time rather than at grant time.
environment: Unity Catalog enabled workspaces. Lakehouse Runtime 11.3 LTS and above.
resolution:
1. Verify the full privilege chain
Run these three checks and confirm the principal appears in each:
SHOW GRANTS ON CATALOG main;
SHOW GRANTS ON SCHEMA main.sales;
SHOW GRANTS ON TABLE main.sales.transactions;

2. Grant the missing traversal privileges
GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG main TO `data-analysts`;
GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA main.sales TO `data-analysts`;
GRANT SELECT ON TABLE main.sales.transactions TO `data-analysts`;

Grant to a group rather than an individual user so the pattern scales.

3. Confirm the cluster access mode
Open the cluster configuration and check Access Mode. It must be Shared or Single User. No Isolation Shared clusters cannot query Unity Catalog objects.

4. For external tables, check the storage credential
SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION `sales_landing`;
The principal needs READ FILES on the external location that backs the table.

5. Confirm the effective identity
Have the user run SELECT current_user(), is_account_group_member('data-analysts'); to verify they are resolving to the identity you granted and are actually in the group.

title: Delta ConcurrentAppendException on concurrent writes to the same table
summary: Two jobs commit to the same Delta table at the same time and one is rejected by optimistic concurrency control. The fix is usually to partition the writes so they touch disjoint files, not to serialize the jobs.
issue:
A write to a Delta table fails with:

io.delta.exceptions.ConcurrentAppendException: Files were added to partition [date=2026-07-14] by a concurrent update. Please try the operation again.

or the related

io.delta.exceptions.ConcurrentDeleteReadException
io.delta.exceptions.MetadataChangedException

The failure is intermittent and correlates with overlapping job schedules.
cause:
Delta Lake uses optimistic concurrency control. Each writer reads a snapshot, stages its changes, and then validates at commit time that no conflicting change landed in between. When two writers touch the same set of files, the second commit is rejected.

ConcurrentAppendException specifically means another transaction added files that the failing transaction's read predicate would have matched. If both writers target the same partition, or if either writer's MERGE or DELETE has no partition predicate, the conflict surface is the entire table.
environment: Delta Lake on all Lakehouse Runtime versions. Most frequently seen with concurrent MERGE operations from streaming and batch pipelines writing to a shared silver table.
resolution:
1. Add partition predicates to every conflicting write
This is the real fix. If two jobs write different dates, make that explicit in the condition so Delta can prove the file sets are disjoint:
MERGE INTO target t USING source s
ON t.date = '2026-07-14' AND t.id = s.id
WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *

Without t.date = ... in the ON clause, Delta must assume the merge could touch any partition and will conflict with any concurrent writer.

2. Confirm the table is partitioned on the isolating column
DESCRIBE DETAIL my_table;
Check partitionColumns. A predicate on a non-partition column does not reduce the conflict surface.

3. Enable deletion vectors and row tracking where available
On DBR 14.3+ with deletion vectors enabled, row-level concurrency significantly reduces conflicts between MERGE and UPDATE operations:
ALTER TABLE my_table SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableDeletionVectors' = 'true');

4. Add bounded retry as a safety net, not a solution
Wrap the write in a retry with exponential backoff and a low cap (3 attempts). Retries mask the symptom; the partition predicate removes the cause.

5. If writes genuinely must be serialized
Stagger the job schedules or route both writers through a single streaming job with foreachBatch.

title: Cluster terminated with INIT_SCRIPT_FAILURE
summary: A cluster-scoped init script exits non-zero or times out, and the platform terminates the cluster before it reaches RUNNING. The script's stdout and stderr are written to the cluster log destination.
issue:
A cluster fails to start with:

TERMINATED: INIT_SCRIPT_FAILURE
Cluster scoped init script <path> failed: Script exit status is non-zero

The cluster may have started successfully for weeks before beginning to fail, with no change to the cluster configuration.
cause:
The init script returned a non-zero exit code or exceeded the init script timeout. Common triggers:

1. Unpinned package installs. A script running pip install somelib without a version constraint starts failing when a new release breaks compatibility with the runtime's Python version. This explains the classic 'it worked yesterday' report.
2. Network egress blocked. The script reaches out to PyPI, Maven Central, or an internal artifact repository that the workspace VPC cannot reach.
3. Script stored in an unreadable location after a migration, for example a DBFS path that moved to a Unity Catalog volume.
4. Runtime upgrade. A script compiled against or assuming an older DBR base image fails on a new LTS.
environment: All Lakehouse Runtime versions. Init scripts on DBFS are deprecated in favor of workspace files and Unity Catalog volumes.
resolution:
1. Read the actual script output
The error in the UI only says the script failed. The reason is in the logs. Go to the cluster's Driver Logs, or to the cluster log delivery destination, and open:
<log-destination>/<cluster-id>/init_scripts/
Each script has its own stdout and stderr file with a timestamped name.

2. Pin every package version
Change pip install requests to pip install requests==2.31.0. Unpinned installs in init scripts are the leading cause of sudden, unexplained cluster start failures.

3. Make the script fail loudly and early
Start the script with set -euxo pipefail so the failing command and its output appear in stderr instead of being silently swallowed.

4. Verify network reachability
Add a reachability probe before the install and check it in the log:
curl -sSf https://pypi.org/simple/ > /dev/null || echo "PYPI UNREACHABLE"

5. Migrate off DBFS init scripts
Move the script to a workspace file or a Unity Catalog volume and update the cluster configuration. DBFS-hosted init scripts are disabled on newer runtimes.

6. Prefer cluster libraries where possible
If the script only installs packages, replace it with cluster libraries or a notebook-scoped %pip install. Libraries surface installation errors far more clearly than init scripts.

title: Library installation failed on cluster
summary: A cluster library stays in FAILED state, usually because of a dependency conflict with a package already present in the Lakehouse Runtime, or because the artifact repository is unreachable.
issue:
A library attached to a cluster shows status Failed and the job using it fails with an import error:

Library installation attempted on the driver node and failed. Error code: ERROR_CODE_LIBRARY_INSTALLATION_FAILURE
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyarrow'

or a Maven library fails with:

Library resolution failed. Cause: java.lang.RuntimeException: unresolved dependency
cause:
Three distinct failure modes share this symptom:

1. Dependency conflict with the runtime. Every Lakehouse Runtime ships a fixed set of Python and JVM libraries. Installing a package that requires a different version of an already-present dependency (pyarrow, pandas, numpy, and jackson are the frequent offenders) causes pip or Maven to fail resolution, or worse, to succeed and then break Spark at runtime.
2. Repository unreachable. The workspace has no egress to PyPI or Maven Central, or an internal proxy requires credentials the cluster does not have.
3. Wrong artifact for the runtime. A Scala 2.12 JAR on a Scala 2.13 runtime, or a wheel built for an incompatible Python version.
environment: All Lakehouse Runtime versions. Conflicts are most common on runtimes that ship a recent pandas or pyarrow, since many data libraries pin those tightly.
resolution:
1. Read the full installation error
Click the failed library in the cluster Libraries tab and expand the message. The pip resolver output names the specific conflicting requirement.

2. Check what the runtime already ships
Look up the System Environment section of the release notes for your DBR version, or run in a notebook:
%pip list | grep -i pyarrow
Then constrain your library to a version compatible with what is already there.

3. Match the artifact to the runtime
For Maven libraries, confirm the Scala version suffix matches the runtime, for example _2.12 on DBR 13.3 LTS. For wheels, confirm the Python version tag.

4. Prefer notebook-scoped installs for iteration
Use %pip install package==1.2.3 in the notebook. This isolates the install to the notebook session, does not require a cluster restart, and gives immediate, readable resolver output.

5. For unreachable repositories
Confirm the cluster can reach the index, then configure the private index explicitly:
%pip install --index-url https://artifacts.internal/simple mypackage==1.0.0
Store credentials in a secret scope rather than inline.

6. For persistent conflicts, containerize
Use Container Services with a custom image where the dependency set is resolved once at build time instead of at every cluster start.

title: SQL Warehouse JDBC or ODBC connection timeout
summary: A BI tool or external client cannot connect to a SQL Warehouse, or times out on first query. Usually the warehouse is stopped and cold-starting, or the client is missing an authentication or network path.
issue:
A JDBC or ODBC client fails to connect to a SQL Warehouse:

[Lakehouse][JDBCDriver](500593) Communication link failure. Failed to connect to server. Reason: HTTP Response code: 503
java.net.SocketTimeoutException: Read timed out
[Simba][ThriftExtension] (14) Unexpected response from server during a HTTP connection: Bad Gateway

The same warehouse works from the SQL editor.
cause:
In order of frequency:

1. Cold start. A stopped serverless or pro warehouse takes time to provision. Clients with a short login timeout give up before the warehouse is ready, and the 503 is the load balancer responding while startup is in progress.
2. Missing or expired credential. A personal access token that has expired, or an OAuth flow that was never completed. This usually surfaces as a 401 but some drivers report it as a link failure.
3. Network path. IP access lists on the workspace, Private Link configuration, or a corporate firewall blocking port 443 to the workspace hostname.
4. Wrong connection parameters. The HTTP Path copied from a cluster instead of a warehouse, or a stale hostname after a workspace migration.
environment: All SQL Warehouse types. Serverless warehouses start fastest; classic warehouses can take several minutes from cold.
resolution:
1. Confirm the warehouse is running
Open SQL Warehouses in the workspace. If it is Stopped, start it and wait for Running before retrying the client. Then set the warehouse auto-stop to a value that matches the reporting schedule, or leave it running during business hours.

2. Raise the client login timeout
Most drivers default to 30 seconds, which is shorter than a classic warehouse cold start. Set the connection timeout to 300 seconds and enable retry on the client side.

3. Verify the connection details exactly
In the warehouse, open Connection Details and copy Server Hostname and HTTP Path verbatim. The HTTP Path for a warehouse looks like /sql/1.0/warehouses/<id>. A path containing /protocolv1/o/ is a cluster path and will not work.

4. Test the credential independently
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" https://<workspace-host>/api/2.0/sql/warehouses
A 401 confirms a token problem rather than a network problem. Regenerate the personal access token if it has expired.

5. Check network controls
If the workspace uses IP access lists, confirm the client's egress IP is allowed. If it uses Private Link, confirm the client resolves the workspace hostname to the private endpoint.

6. Upgrade the driver
Older Simba drivers have known issues with newer warehouse versions. Move to a current JDBC or ODBC driver release.

title: Structured Streaming fails with checkpoint or offset mismatch
summary: A streaming query will not restart because its checkpoint no longer matches the query plan or the source offsets. Never delete a checkpoint without understanding the data consequences.
issue:
A Structured Streaming job fails on restart with one of:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Error reading delta file .../state/0/12/1.delta of HDFSStateStoreProvider
org.apache.spark.sql.streaming.StreamingQueryException: Cannot find earliest offsets of Set(topic-0). Some data may have been missed.
java.lang.IllegalStateException: batch 4821 doesn't exist
Query [id = ...] terminated with exception: Provided schema doesn't match the schema in the checkpoint
cause:
The checkpoint directory is the durable identity of a streaming query. It stores the query plan, the source offsets processed so far, and any stateful operator state. The query refuses to start when these no longer reconcile:

1. Query plan changed incompatibly. Adding or removing a stateful operator, changing the output mode, or altering the aggregation keys invalidates the stored state.
2. Source data aged out. Kafka retention expired past the committed offset, or files tracked in the source log were deleted.
3. Two queries sharing one checkpoint. Two concurrent runs of the same job write conflicting entries.
4. Checkpoint on non-durable or partially deleted storage.
environment: Structured Streaming on all Lakehouse Runtime versions. Auto Loader and Kafka sources are the most common contexts.
resolution:
1. Establish which failure you have before touching anything
Read the exception carefully. A state-store read error is a corruption or plan-change problem. An offset-not-found error is a retention problem. They have different consequences.

2. For a plan change, plan a controlled restart
Stateful query plans cannot be migrated. Decide whether you can reprocess from the source. If you can, start the query with a new checkpoint location and a defined starting position:
.option("checkpointLocation", "/Volumes/main/ops/checkpoints/job_v2")
.option("startingOffsets", "earliest")
Keep the old checkpoint directory until the new run is validated.

3. For Kafka retention loss, decide explicitly on data loss
Setting failOnDataLoss to false will let the query resume by skipping the missing range. Only do this if skipping data is acceptable, and record what was skipped:
.option("failOnDataLoss", "false")
Otherwise, restore the data from an archive and replay it.

4. Confirm only one writer owns the checkpoint
Check for a second job or a manually started notebook stream using the same path. Each streaming query needs its own checkpoint location.

5. Verify checkpoint durability
Checkpoints must live on durable cloud storage or a Unity Catalog volume, never on local disk or ephemeral scratch.

6. Prevent recurrence
Version the checkpoint path alongside the query code, so an intentional plan change gets a new checkpoint by construction rather than by incident response.

title: FetchFailedException during shuffle read
summary: A stage fails while fetching shuffle blocks from another executor. The shuffle service could not serve the block, typically because the source executor died or the node was reclaimed.
issue:
A job fails during a wide transformation with:

org.apache.spark.shuffle.FetchFailedException: Failed to connect to ip-10-0-3-42.ec2.internal:4048
Caused by: java.io.IOException: Connection reset by peer

or

FetchFailedException: java.lang.RuntimeException: Executor is not registered

Spark retries the parent stage, and the job either recovers slowly or aborts after repeated attempts.
cause:
A FetchFailedException means an executor could not read shuffle output from a peer. It is a downstream symptom, not the root cause. The real reason is one of:

1. The source executor died. Usually an OOM kill, which appears earlier in the log as an ExecutorLostFailure. Its shuffle files went with it.
2. The node was reclaimed. Spot or preemptible instance reclamation removes a node mid-shuffle.
3. Disk exhaustion. Shuffle spill filled the local disks, so writes failed and the blocks were never complete.
4. Network saturation on very large shuffles, causing connection timeouts.
environment: All Lakehouse Runtime versions. Strongly correlated with spot instance usage and with jobs that shuffle more data than the cluster's aggregate local disk.
resolution:
1. Look earlier in the log, not at the fetch failure
Search the driver log for the first ExecutorLostFailure or Executor decommissioned before the fetch error. That line names the real cause.

2. If executors were OOM killed
Follow the executor memory guidance: check for skew first, then raise spark.executor.memoryOverhead, then move to a memory-optimized node type.

3. If nodes were reclaimed
Reduce the spot ratio, or run the driver and a baseline of workers on-demand. Enable decommissioning so shuffle data migrates off a node before it is removed:
spark.decommission.enabled true
spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled true

4. If local disk filled
Check the Spark UI executor tab for shuffle spill volume. Move to a node type with more local SSD, or reduce the shuffle size by filtering and projecting earlier in the pipeline.

5. Reduce shuffle volume structurally
Push filters before joins, select only required columns, and let adaptive query execution coalesce partitions:
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled", true)

6. Raise fetch tolerance only as a stopgap
spark.reducer.maxReqsInFlight 4 and a longer spark.network.timeout can help a marginal job complete, but they do not address why executors are dying.

title: S3 AccessDenied 403 reading or writing external data
summary: A job cannot read or write an S3 path because the cluster's instance profile, the bucket policy, or the KMS key policy denies the request. The three must all agree.
issue:
A read or write to S3 fails with:

java.nio.file.AccessDeniedException: s3a://prod-lakehouse/bronze/events: getFileStatus on s3a://prod-lakehouse/bronze/events: com.amazonaws.services.s3.model.AmazonS3Exception: Forbidden (Service: Amazon S3; Status Code: 403; Error Code: 403 Forbidden)

or

com.amazonaws.services.s3.model.AmazonS3Exception: Access Denied (Service: Amazon S3; Status Code: 403; Error Code: AccessDenied)

The same path may be readable from another cluster.
cause:
An S3 403 is the intersection of three independent authorization layers, and any one of them can deny:

1. The IAM role attached to the cluster (instance profile, or the storage credential for Unity Catalog external locations) lacks the required s3 action on that prefix.
2. The bucket policy does not allow the role's principal, or explicitly denies it. Cross-account access requires both sides.
3. The KMS key policy does not grant the role kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey for an SSE-KMS encrypted bucket. This produces a 403 on the object even when S3 permissions are correct, and is the least obvious of the three.

A fourth cause on Unity Catalog workspaces: the path is governed by an external location the principal has no READ FILES grant on.
environment: AWS workspaces. Applies to both instance profile clusters and Unity Catalog storage credentials.
resolution:
1. Identify which identity is actually being used
On a UC cluster the storage credential's role is used, not the instance profile. Confirm in the cluster configuration and in the external location definition. Debugging the wrong role is the most common time sink here.

2. Check the IAM policy covers the exact prefix
The policy needs s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject on arn:aws:s3:::prod-lakehouse/bronze/* and s3:ListBucket on arn:aws:s3:::prod-lakehouse with a matching prefix condition. A ListBucket grant without the object-level grant produces a 403 on read.

3. Check the KMS key policy
If the bucket uses SSE-KMS, the role needs kms:Decrypt for reads and both kms:Decrypt and kms:GenerateDataKey for writes, granted on the key itself. Verify with:
aws kms get-key-policy --key-id <id> --policy-name default

4. Check the bucket policy for cross-account or explicit deny
An explicit Deny anywhere overrides every Allow. Look for deny statements conditioned on aws:SourceVpce or aws:PrincipalOrgID.

5. For Unity Catalog, check the grant
SHOW GRANTS ON EXTERNAL LOCATION `bronze_events`;
Grant READ FILES or WRITE FILES to the principal as needed.

6. Validate from the cluster
Run dbutils.fs.ls("s3a://prod-lakehouse/bronze/") in a notebook on the same cluster. This isolates a credential problem from a job-specific problem.

title: Delta MERGE fails with schema mismatch or ambiguous reference
summary: A MERGE INTO fails because the source and target schemas diverged, or because the merge condition does not uniquely match target rows.
issue:
A MERGE operation fails with one of:

AnalysisException: A schema mismatch detected when writing to the Delta table.
To enable schema migration using DataFrameWriter or DataStreamWriter, please set: '.option("mergeSchema", "true")'

DeltaAnalysisException: Cannot resolve column 'customer_tier' in the target table

UnsupportedOperationException: Cannot perform Merge as multiple source rows matched and attempted to modify the same target row in the Delta table.
cause:
Two unrelated problems present under the same operation:

1. Schema divergence. The upstream source added, removed, or retyped a column. Delta enforces schema on write by design, so the write is rejected rather than silently coerced. A widened type such as int to long is still a mismatch.

2. Non-unique merge keys. The multiple-source-rows error means the ON condition matched more than one source row to a single target row. Delta cannot decide which update wins, so it refuses. This is a data quality problem in the source, most often duplicate change-data-capture events for the same primary key within one batch.
environment: Delta Lake on all Lakehouse Runtime versions. Schema evolution behavior differs slightly across versions; automatic merge schema for MERGE requires DBR 9.1 LTS or later.
resolution:
1. Diff the schemas before changing any settings
DESCRIBE TABLE target_table;
and inspect source_df.printSchema(). Identify exactly which column differs and whether it is new, removed, or retyped.

2. For an intentional new column, enable schema evolution deliberately
SET spark.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled = true;
Scope this to the specific job rather than setting it cluster-wide. Enabling it globally means an upstream typo silently adds a column to a governed table.

3. For an unintended change, fix the source
If the column appeared because of an upstream schema drift, cast explicitly in the source query so the contract stays stable:
SELECT id, CAST(amount AS DECIMAL(18,2)) AS amount FROM staging

4. For the multiple-matched-rows error, deduplicate the source
Keep only the latest record per key before merging:
WITH ranked AS (
SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY id ORDER BY event_ts DESC) rn
FROM source
)
SELECT * EXCEPT(rn) FROM ranked WHERE rn = 1

5. Confirm the merge key is genuinely unique in the target
SELECT id, COUNT(*) c FROM target_table GROUP BY id HAVING c > 1;
Duplicates in the target indicate an earlier merge already ran without a unique key.

6. Add a constraint to catch it next time
ALTER TABLE target_table ADD CONSTRAINT id_not_null CHECK (id IS NOT NULL);

title: Job instability caused by spot instance reclamation
summary: Long-running jobs fail intermittently because spot or preemptible workers are reclaimed by the cloud provider mid-stage. The symptom is executor loss with no application error.
issue:
A job that normally succeeds fails intermittently. The driver log shows executors disappearing with no application-level exception:

WARN TaskSetManager: Lost task 218.0 in stage 9.0: ExecutorLostFailure (executor 12 exited unrelated to the running tasks) Reason: Worker lost
INFO StandaloneSchedulerBackend: Executor 12 decommissioned
Cluster event: SPOT_INSTANCE_TERMINATION

Failures cluster around specific times of day and are more frequent for longer jobs.
cause:
Spot and preemptible instances are reclaimed by the cloud provider with minimal notice when on-demand demand rises. The probability that a job is hit scales with both its duration and its worker count, which is why long ETL runs fail while short interactive queries appear fine.

Two aggravating factors:

1. The driver is on spot. Losing the driver kills the entire application with no recovery. Losing a worker only costs a stage retry.
2. Shuffle data is lost with the node, which triggers cascading FetchFailedException retries in downstream stages.
environment: AWS spot instances, Azure spot VMs, GCP preemptible VMs. Applies to both all-purpose and job clusters configured with spot workers.
resolution:
1. Confirm reclamation is the cause
Open the cluster Event Log and look for SPOT_INSTANCE_TERMINATION events correlated with the failure time. If they are absent, the executor loss has a different cause and you should investigate memory instead.

2. Put the driver on-demand, always
In the cluster configuration set the driver to on-demand even when workers are spot. This single change converts most total job failures into recoverable stage retries.

3. Set a hybrid worker mix
Configure a number of on-demand workers sufficient to hold the job's baseline, with spot for the elastic portion. On AWS this is the 'first N on-demand' setting.

4. Enable graceful decommissioning
Let Spark migrate shuffle and cached blocks off a node when a reclamation notice arrives:
spark.decommission.enabled true
spark.storage.decommission.enabled true
spark.storage.decommission.shuffleBlocks.enabled true
spark.storage.decommission.rddBlocks.enabled true

5. For business-critical jobs, stop using spot
Compute cost saved is not worth an unreliable nightly load. Reserve spot for development, ad-hoc analysis, and idempotent jobs that can safely retry.

6. Checkpoint long pipelines
Break a multi-hour job into stages that write intermediate Delta tables, so a failure resumes from the last completed stage rather than from the beginning.

title: Driver unresponsive and notebook detached due to GC thrashing
summary: The driver spends nearly all its time in garbage collection, stops responding to heartbeats, and the notebook detaches. Distinct from an outright OOM, though it usually precedes one.
issue:
A notebook detaches mid-execution and the cluster reports:

The spark driver has stopped unexpectedly and is restarting. Your notebook will be automatically reattached.
Driver is up but is not responsive, likely due to GC.

The driver log shows sustained full GC activity:

[Full GC (Allocation Failure) 27829M->27604M(28160M), 12.4471030 secs]
[Full GC (Allocation Failure) 27604M->27811M(28160M), 13.9982211 secs]

Each collection reclaims almost nothing and takes longer than the last.
cause:
The driver heap is nearly full and the JVM is in a GC death spiral: it collects continuously, frees very little, and has no cycles left for application work or heartbeats. The platform marks the driver unresponsive and restarts it.

Root causes are the same set as driver OOM but reached more gradually:

1. Accumulating state across cells. Long-lived interactive sessions build up cached DataFrames, large Python objects, and query results that are never released.
2. Many concurrent notebooks on one driver. All-purpose clusters share a single driver JVM across every attached notebook.
3. Large results held for display. Repeatedly calling display() on wide result sets retains them.
4. Driver-side single-node libraries such as pandas or scikit-learn operating on data sized for the cluster rather than for one machine.
environment: All Lakehouse Runtime versions. Predominantly on shared all-purpose clusters used interactively over long sessions.
resolution:
1. Confirm the pattern in the driver log
Look for consecutive Full GC (Allocation Failure) lines where the post-collection heap barely drops. That signature distinguishes GC thrashing from a single allocation spike.

2. Release accumulated state
In the affected notebook:
spark.catalog.clearCache()
and delete large Python variables explicitly with del. Detaching and reattaching the notebook is the blunt version of this and is a valid immediate mitigation.

3. Reduce concurrency on the driver
Count the notebooks attached to the cluster. Move heavy users to their own clusters, or move scheduled work to job clusters so it does not share a driver with interactive users.

4. Size the driver for driver work
If the workload legitimately does single-node processing with pandas, choose a memory-optimized driver. Adding workers does nothing for this failure.

5. Move single-node work to the cluster
Replace pandas operations on full datasets with Spark DataFrame operations, or use pandas API on Spark so the work distributes.

6. Prevent recurrence
Set cluster auto-termination so long interactive sessions do not accumulate state indefinitely, and use job clusters for anything scheduled.
